World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Mapping the most critical shipping lanes in the world
World.content:
For almost two months the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most crucial shipping routes, has been effectively blocked as a result of the Iran war.

Oil prices have spiked, inflation fears have risen and the global economy has been shaken.

A fifth of the world's oil output — and 11 per cent of all seaborne trade — is shipped via the narrow stretch separating the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Aden.

Experts fear that by taking control of the strait, Iran may be opening the door to a dangerous and costly new era of maritime trade, where long-standing conventions and treaties are not followed.

In recent weeks, the US also declared it would restrict maritime movement through the strait.

Iran war live updates: For the latest news on the Middle East crisis, read our blog.

The Strait of Hormuz is not alone in being a vital route to move goods by sea.

About 90 per cent of all traded goods are shipped by sea, and there are 13 key choke points around the world that roughly three-quarters of that global maritime trade passes though.

Among them, five are considered the most important for global trade by economic and security experts.

When Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz by reportedly placing sea mines, threatening attacks on vessels attempting to pass without permission from the Iranian government, and even charging or threatening to charge a toll on passing traffic, decades of international shipping conventions were thrown out.

One ship paid $US2m to pass Iran. Now we're looking at a new era If Iran's idea of charging ships to pass through maritime choke points catches on, we are entering a new era of much more expensive, more dangerous global shipping.

Australian National University's Donald Rothwell, an expert in international law, said it could set a dangerous precedent and further disrupt global trade.

The United Nations Convention on Law of the Sea protects the rights of ships and aircraft to transit through international straits, which includes the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran abided by that convention for decades prior to the war, despite not being a signatory, he said.

But Professor Rothwell is concerned about what impact the introduction of a toll may have on other international straits.

Yesterday, Indonesia's finance minister suggested tolls could be levied on ships using the Malacca Strait.

"There is a potential that other countries who border significant straits will also give some consideration to whether or not they can also impose some form of toll," he said.

There's a long history of conflict and tensions in these strategically valuable straits, so where are they and how did they become so important?

Where is the Strait of Malacca?

More than 90,000 ships sail through the Strait of Malacca every year, transporting 30 per cent of the world's traded goods, according to the World Economic Forum.

It's a critical bottleneck for Asian trade, but especially for China.

Two thirds of Chinese trade, including 80 per cent of its energy imports, are carried on ships through the strait each year.

It is also the shortest shipping route between East Asia, the Middle East and Europe, connecting the Indian Ocean with the South China Sea.

The strait, nestled between Malaysia, Indonesia and Singapore, has about 45 per cent of the world's seaborne oil transit through each year.

It also sees significant volumes of soybeans and rice transported through it each year, according to Chatham House.

Asia's dominance of global manufacturing means any disruptions to marine traffic in the strait would create problems for economies all over the world, according to University of Melbourne Supply chain expert Mehrdokht Pournader.

"So if the strait of Malacca is disrupted, then it means that the world's factory and the world's manufacturing is going to be disrupted," she said.

" So some straits are more critical than the others and Strait of Malacca is one of them. "

Defence expert and former naval officer Jennifer Parker said given the volume of trade that transited the choke point, any disruption would be significant.

But unlike the Strait of Hormuz, ships can take alternative routes to avoid the Strait of Malacca.

"One of the trade-offs with that alternative is that it adds distance," she said.

"If trade was stopped through the strait of Malacca, then you would have a shortage of suppliers getting into South-East Asia and North-East Asia in a timely fashion.

"You would have a shortage of supplies coming out of South-East Asia. So a lot of [Australia's] refined fuel, for example."

Where is the Suez Canal?

Tens of thousands of ships transit the narrow Egyptian-controlled waterway that links the Red Sea and the Mediterranean.

The trip can shave at least 10 days off travel between Asia and Europe by avoiding sailing around South Africa.

It represents about 10 per cent of global seaborne trade, including about 20 per cent of car shipments, 22 per cent of container traffic and 10 per cent of oil.

It's also an important trade route for fertiliser produced in Eastern Europe and shipped to China, one of the world's biggest fertiliser importers, according to analysis by Chatham House.

In 2021, a container ship held up traffic on the choke point for about six days after getting stuck sideways.

Evergreen Marine Corporation, the Taiwan-based shipping company that operates the vessel, blamed strong winds for the ship being stuck in the Suez Canal. (AP: Suez Canal Authority)

Houthi attacks nearly 300 kilometres to the south of the Suez Canal led to significant drop in traffic.

In 2023, the number of ships going through the waterway was more than 26,000. The following year, that fell to about 13,000, but there are alternative routes.

"The way you get around going through the Suez Canal, or in fact, the Bab el-Mandeb is going around the Cape of Good Hope [in South Africa]," Ms Parker said.

" But those alternative routes, the trade-off is it adds time and it adds costs; an extra 14 days, on average. "

Where is the Bab el-Mandeb Strait?

The shipping lane between Yemen and Djibouti connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, and is critical for the export of oil and natural gas from the Middle East.

It represents about 8.7 per cent of global seaborne trade including 20 per cent of both cars and container traffic and 13 per cent of oil.

But from late 2023, Houthi forces attacked ships passing the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, where the bulk of vessels transiting the Suez Canal travel from.

Loading...

Ms Parker said the rerouting of ships to the Cape of Good Hope near South Africa had led to a domino effect in other parts of the world.

"What you started to see is delays in the port of Singapore because ships were arriving at different times, so Singapore was backed up during that period," she said.

" You start to see shortages of supplies. You also start to see build-up of trade in different ports. "

"So these things always have a flow-on effect to maritime trade and the maritime trade ecosystem generally."

Dr Pournader agreed, saying this could create what was known as a "bullwhip effect", which is when small changes in consumer demand result in large changes at the wholesaler level, altering how supply chains operate.

"So whatever disruption that you have at the beginning of your supply chain, then that disruption exponentially grows down the supply chain for manufacturing, for how long it will take for the customers to get goods," Ms Parker said.

"So if you have a delay of one week in getting your commodities or the fuel, that delay can grow into multiple weeks until the commodity gets to the customer."

Where are the Turkish Straits?

The Turkish Straits, the Bosporus and Dardanelles, is the only maritime passage route between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean, and is controlled by Türkiye.

About 3 per cent of goods traded by sea, including roughly a fifth of the world's wheat exports, are shipped through this waterway each year.

About 77 per cent of wheat exports from Russia, Ukraine and Kazakhstan pass through it, while about 39 per cent of those exports transit through both the Suez Canal and Bab el-Mandab Strait, according to analysis by Chatham House.

The world is facing a perfect storm The ripple effects of concurrent crises are leading the world on a path to crushing hunger — and the possibility of more war.

At the beginning of Russia's war in Ukraine, there were food security fears surrounding Ukraine as the fifth-largest exporter of wheat.

Prior to the war, Ukraine's wheat exports supplied 38 per cent of African countries.

Middle Eastern nations were also highly reliant on Black Sea grain imports.

"Before Ukraine got the upper hand in the Black Sea … we saw the impact on global food supply," Ms Parker said.

"The Turkish Straits, the Bosporus and Dardanelles, are true choke points like the Strait of Hormuz in terms of there's no other maritime alternative.

" That is the only entry in and out of the Black Sea. "

Where is the Panama Canal?

The waterway connecting the Pacific and Atlantic oceans accounts for about 2.5 per cent of global seaborne trade.

Despite representing a small share of the bulk of maritime trade, it is strategically important to countries such as the United States, carrying about 40 per cent of the US's containerised goods.

It is also crucial for the US's agricultural exports, such as maize and soybean, as those goods transit the waterway to get to Asia.

After its construction by the United States in the early 1900s, control over the canal was formally handed over to Panama more than four decades ago.

But US president Donald Trump's has vowed to "take back" the waterway, claiming it had been under China's control.

Loading...

Outside of geopolitics, there have been growing concerns about the long-term health of the waterway.

The Panama Canal is supplied by fresh water from Lake Gatún, unlike the Suez Canal, which is supplied by sea water.

But there has been a sharp decline in fresh water in recent years due to severe droughts, which led to a 30 per cent of drop in traffic on the waterway in 2023.

Ms Parker said disruption to the ships transiting the Panama Canal would significantly impact the US, but said alternatives to the choke point existed.

"You can go around the south of South America, to Cape Horn. That's quite a rough transit and it'll add to one to two weeks of transit time," she said.

"The other option is you could actually go the other way around and send things through the Suez Canal, but that adds a significant amount of time."

Dr Pournader said despite alternatives, disruptions caused issues with the larger maritime ecosystem.

"If it is disrupted, then agricultural exports again are going to be disrupted, consumer goods are going to be disrupted," she said.

World.title: Law firm ordered to pay more than $4.7m after overcharging outback council
World.content:
A NSW Supreme Court judge has ordered a Sydney-based law firm and some related companies to pay more than $4.7 million to the Broken Hill City Council.

It comes almost a month after Justice Elizabeth Peden ruled the council had been "mostly successful" in its claims against former legal provider Redenbach Legal, which it took to court for alleged overcharging.

Submission of the final orders had been postponed pending further discussions between the parties, with Justice Peden holding a further hearing last week before issuing her final decision on April 16.

Justice Peden also ordered the Redenbach parties to cover the legal fees of the council, and its current and former general managers, who had been subject to a now-dismissed cross-claim.

A civil hearing between the parties took place in Sydney between February and March. (ABC News: Jak Rowland)

Relationship sours over alleged overcharging

Proceedings were first launched in 2023, with the council looking to recoup some of its legal fees from Redenbach Legal and its principal solicitor, Keith Redenbach.

However, council general manager Jay Nankivell said the case's history actually went back close to 10 years.

"[It] initially started with the incomplete build of the Broken Hill Civic Centre renovations," Mr Nankivell said.

"There was obviously the ombudsman investigation that was looped into that as well, at the same time, complicating matters, so that was the best part of five years in regards to legal action there."

It is understood the dispute was tied to litigation over renovations to the city's civic centre. (ABC Broken Hill: Bill Ormonde)

Mr Nankivell said the action was undertaken by Mr Redenbach and his firm, initially under the name Redenbach Lee Lawyers, in the council's disputes with architecture firm Allen Jack+Cottier, now known as AJC Architects, and builder Unique Urban Built.

However, when the council finally received its bill of costs in 2022 from Passer Par, a company understood to also be affiliated with Mr Redenbach, it found the fees eclipsed the settlement it had received from the architects.

Broken Hill Mayor Tom Kennedy has previously reported that the council's total fees exceeded $10 million, incurred over several years and legal matters.

Mr Nankivell has confirmed the figure, with the total gains and losses to be made public in a report at an upcoming council meeting.

Judge mostly sides with council

Subsequent civil action between the council and Redenbach parties was ultimately heard in the Supreme Court over several days between February 23 and March 12 this year.

Proceedings also included a cross-claim from the Redenbach parties against the council, Mr Nankivell and former general manager James Roncon over claimed unpaid invoices.

However, in her initial March 25 judgment, Justice Peden dismissed this cross-claim and found mostly in favour of the council, while also referring to Mr Redenbach as a "thoroughly unimpressive witness".

Jay Nankivell gave evidence in the hearing on behalf of the council. (Supplied: Broken Hill City Council)

Then, in her later April 16 judgment, she described the conduct displayed by the Redenbach parties throughout litigation as "unreasonable", ruling they should pay the legal costs of the council, Mr Nankivell and Mr Roncon on an indemnity basis.

Mr Nankivell said in total, the council was awarded a settlement worth close to $4 million, including costs, plus more than $786,000 in pre-judgement interest, which was a "fantastic outcome".

"[It was] certainly a big relief for all of the councillors involved that'd gone down this process for the last few years [in] recouping this money," he said.

" It ended up being a settlement and a win [that was] better than what council had anticipated. "

Mr Nankivell said the council was also entitled to further costs for work not done, which would be determined separately by an independent cost assessor.

The now-closed Redenbach Legal offices on Broken Hill's main street. (ABC News: Oliver Brown)

Appeal window open

Although the final judgement has been handed down, the Redenbach parties can appeal the decision if they believe there was a legal or factual error committed during the process.

Generally, a notice of intention to appeal needs to be filed within 28 days after the judgement is handed down.

The ABC contacted Redenbach Legal for comment, specifically asking if it or Mr Redenbach intended to appeal, but did not receive a response.

World.title: Two charged after $13m drug seizure on Hume Highway
World.content:
Two people have been charged after police allegedly found $13 million worth of methylamphetamine hidden in a car in regional Victoria.

A 22-year-old man and 24-year-old woman from Hillsdale in NSW were arrested after officers intercepted a car on the Hume Highway in Wangaratta.

During a search of the vehicle, police allegedly seized 33kg of methylamphetamine.

The pair were charged with trafficking a large commercial drug of dependence and are expected to appear before the Wangaratta Magistrates Court today.

Police said the arrests came after an investigation into drug trafficking between NSW and Victoria.

Detective Inspector Jamie Walker from Victoria Police's Major Drug Squad said combating drugs remained a major focus of the force.

"We have zero tolerance for those bringing harm to our community by importing and trafficking drugs of any kind," Detective Inspector Walker said.

Drugs were a major driver of crime, and the arrests were illustrative of police's commitment to combat illicit substance trade in Victoria, he said.

"Our team has relentlessly tracked down offenders as part of this investigation and in turn have removed considerable quantities of drugs from the streets."

World.title: Moloney wins bloodbath as boxing's brutal beauty tested
World.content:
On a bloody Thursday night at Brisbane's Fortitude Music Hall, Jason Moloney overcame a deep cut in the 10th round to keep on track for a return to boxing's highest level with a unanimous points decision victory over American Andre Donovan.

Despite adding his blood to an already splattered ring in Brisbane, Moloney earned 97-92 scores on all three judges' cards in a brutal fight as his awkward American opponent was deducted a point for holding in the eighth round.

"When I saw the little bit of footage of him, I thought, this is the sort of guy that can drag you into a dogfight and make you look real ordinary," the always affable and engaging Moloney told ABC Sport in the ring.

"I thought, if I box him how I know I can, and fight my fight, I can do this comfortably. And I didn't.

Jason Moloney had to work hard to get to grips with Andre Donovan. (ABC Sport: Simon Smale)

"And look, hats off to him. He was obviously very hungry … He was smothering me, he was charging me, he was putting his head in — I just couldn't keep my range and fight my fight.

"But at the top level, man, you've got to be able to do better than that. I'm being hard on myself, I know, but that's why I continue to improve because I'm not satisfied with something like that.

"It was lucky it was only the last round that got the head clash. We hit heads about at least 20 times in there, every time he got in close.

"I wasn't meaning to hold, but I had to stop his head charging to me, or it was going to be a bloodbath."

Fighting is rarely pretty, but even accounting for that, the gruesome reminders of this brutal business left the Fortitude Valley canvas looking like a macabre Jackson Pollock parody.

Conor Wallace had to overcome a grinning Argentine and a brutal gash. (ABC Sport: Simon Smale)

In the co-main event, Conor Wallace was badly split in the fourth round by the head of gurning Argentine Walter Sequeira.

Wallace was using this as a keep-busy contest after 10 months out the ring and, as always, the rangy, Ireland-born light heavyweight bought plenty of entertainment to proceedings.

Sequeira play-acted the clown throughout, grinning and showboating through the first two rounds — Wallace, a willing participant in his comical charade that peaked with both men screaming in each other's faces at the end of the third.

However, the copious blood-letting sharpened both men's focus — a reminder that one doesn't play at boxing — forcing Wallace to work the body to such an extent that Sequeira took a knee in the fifth, and then uttered a final "no more" in the sixth.

Maximum blood-letting from rising star McIntyre

Max McIntyre is a born showman. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

The most bloody fight had taken place earlier, though, when Max McIntyre turned Tej Pratap Singh's nose into a horrifying faucet from their early, showman-like exchanges.

McIntyre is rapidly cultivating a following within Australian boxing circles.

A stylish and classy 21-year-old with fast feet and faster hands, the 192-centimetre-tall McIntyre has stood out since he first stepped into a ring for both his boxing skill, ringcraft and the more intangible quality, presence.

The youngster has proven himself to be an entertainer, that most valuable of commodities in a field of thousands, where any stand-out feature can help elevate a fighter to an enduring spot in fight fans' memories.

There is a degree of arrogance that verges on the unhealthy as McIntyre can't help but showboat — by the end of the first, he was posturing and preening, arms low, hands on hips, in a way completely at odds with the severity of the situation in front of him.

Singh's white shorts were soon splattered with blood that was flowing freely from his nose by the end of the first, blood that was soon also smeared across McIntyre's back and spotting the ring and those in the front row, a sickening reminder of the visceral impact of those bludgeoning fists.

Max McIntyre had to be watchful in what turned into a bloodbath. (ABC Sport: Simon Smale)

A question boxing fans have wrestled with since boxing was first codified, is how can such a violent pursuit ever be considered art; such a blood-flecked portrait of pain ever be considered beautiful?

At his best, McIntyre's youthful flourishes encourage this paradox — and as Singh's blood stained the ring and everyone in it, McIntyre's swiftness, bobbing and darting style revealed that such a furious dance can have joy within it.

Yet last night, he was not quite there, understandable given such a wanton opponent.

Singh's relentless forward pressure belied the visible signs of his discomfort, his blood flecking McIntyre's white shoes and staining his white gloves a nauseating shade of claret over their eight rounds of combat.

It was only in the final round when the towel was thrown in by Singh's corner that the durable opponent was saved at the very end from further punishment when no chance of victory was possible.

McIntyre flexed his hands after they were removed from his gloves as if in awe at what they had been able to dish out without the veteran hitting the canvas.

Nevertheless, McIntyre's knockout streak continues, a 10th professional win with nine coming inside the distance, a record not to be sniffed at.

Suliaman Guushaa stuns in 90-second debut

Suliaman Guushaa's debut packed a hell of a punch. (Supplied: Tasman Fighters)

Sitting ringside at a fight, close enough to see the intense focus revealed in the whites of each fighter's eyes, is an incredibly intimate experience.

The opening bout saw Xavier Fletcher take on Bongani Sibanda in a furious and keenly contested six-round middleweight bout.

The cool environs of the Fortitude Music Hall meant little as the men in the ring went about their visceral work, sweat beading on each fighter's exposed backs, dissipating in a fine mist with each brutal exchange.

Before long, both men's mouths were permanently parted, the bloating caused in part by their mouthguards, but mostly due to their significant exertions.

It was hard to split the fighters' ringside. The judges felt so too — a split decision draw the verdict.

The judge on my side of the ring, Brandon Wood, scored it 58-56 to Sibanda, a score that this reporter was inclined to agree with. Opposite us, though, the score was 57-57, while to our right, Fletcher did enough to earn that judge's approval 59-55.

The next fight was not so close.

Debutant Suliaman Guushaa positively skipped his way into the ring, roared on by a huge amount of support from the balcony.

That support prompted a grin on the young fighter's face as he worked his way into position.

The final few seconds before a fight begins must be of supreme clarity for a fighter.

The support in the stands, the final words of encouragement from the coaches — it's all just background noise before it is you versus the man opposite.

That wry smile from Guushaa betrayed enormous confidence in himself, a reassurance both for himself, for those watching — including his mother at home — that he was in the right place.

Yet after his seconds — Jeff Horn's former trainer Glenn Rushton among them — exited the ring, Guushaa's face resumed its mask of concentration, a hint of apprehension flickering across his furrowed brow as he stared into the face of his opponent.

But the former Australian Golden Glove winner needn't have worried, a thunderous body shot that doubtless could have been heard with brutal clarity even up in the balcony areas, sending Scottie Williams to one knee amidst roars of delight from the crowd inside the opening minute.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

The fight lasted not much longer after that first shot, a 90-second study of unmitigated dominance from the youngster that promises plenty more to come.

The next fights followed a similar vein, Austin Aokuso sending his overmatched Chinese fighter Wulamu Tulake to the canvas two times in short succession to claim the WBC Australasian light heavyweight strap, before Irishman Chris O'Reilly landed a power right flush on Josh Hatherley, sending the Aussie staggering back against the ropes before the referee stepped in to save the clearly stunned fighter from further punishment.

The heavily-muscled man from Drogheda, whose admirable amateur record suggests a successful career in the paid ranks, moved to a professional record of 4-0 to the delight of the multitudinous Irish supporters ringside.

Another with lofty aspirations is Ben Mahoney, who earned a tight unanimous decision over a "shattered" Dan Hill in their IBF Pan-Pacific super welterweight clash.

Mahoney sat back throughout, counter-punching with startling clarity, rapping his shots off the skeletal orbital bones of Hill, who was desperately unhappy about the decision, although few observers aside from the desperately one-eyed could have too much of an issue with the cards of 96-94, 97-93 and 97-93.

World.title: Tradwives, gangsters and one very special dog: April's 10 best books
World.content:
Welcome to the ABC Arts wrap of the best new books out in April.

Our critics' picks this month have something for every type of reader.

In Yesteryear, Caro Claire Burke imagines what would happen if a tradwife influencer woke up one day to find herself living in the 19th century, with hilarious results.

In London Falling, Patrick Radden Keefe's investigation of the mysterious death of a teenager who fell from a luxury apartment building takes him into the city's underworld.

And a prison inmate goes on the run with his canine companion in Good Boy, a moving novel by Australian author Michelle Wright exposing the failings of the criminal justice system.

Happy reading!

Yesteryear by Caro Claire Burke

Fourth Estate

Anne Hathaway is slated to co-produce and star in the film adaptation of Yesteryear. (Supplied: HarperCollins Publishers)

Sometimes a book captures the Zeitgeist, popping up in every literary conversation until you just have to dive in.

Right now, that book is Yesteryear, a buzzy debut that has captured readers in a saturated attention economy with a simple hook: what if a tradwife influencer was forced to live in 'yesteryear'?

Natalie Heller Mills is our unlikeable and unreliable anti-heroine who spends her days showing the world her faultless life. She describes herself wryly as "a flawless Christian woman. The manic Pixie American dream girl of this nation's deepest, darkest fantasies".

She has created an online version of herself where she is a perfect mother, wife and woman.

Natalie is, of course, living a lie. She is determined for her millions of viewers not to see the truth. To achieve this, she hides the insecticides on her organic farm, the fortune she married into that she uses to pave over mistakes, the nannies who care for her children and her disdain for her husband, who is more interested in spending his days on manosphere forums than with her.

Redefining the tradwife movement These women are redefining what it means to be a stay-at-home parent.

Then, one day, she wakes up in 1855 and is forced to put her tradwife skills to the test in a world without electricity and running water — or Instagram. What follows is a dark and twisting yet hilarious narrative exposing the truth behind the carefully curated facade.

Yesteryear interrogates our fascination with the tradwife movement and its signature blend of traditional values, regressive politics and glitzy capitalism.

Are tradwives victims or perpetrators of patriarchy? Are they active participants in their own subjugation, creating unattainable standards and unhealthy narratives for other women to aspire to? Or are they simply deluded in the belief that they are the masters of their fate?

Caro Claire Burke — who co-hosts the pop culture podcast Diabolical Lies — asks big questions about religion, politics, feminism and the fabled American Dream. And while Yesteryear may not answer all the questions it poses, this is a fun, biting and fast-paced read that is perfect fodder for debate.

— Rosie Ofori Ward

A Rising of the Lights by Steve Toltz

Penguin

"If you can't find the humour in difficult circumstances, then the misery will just be compounded," Toltz told ABC Radio National's The Book Show. (Supplied: Penguin Books Australia)

Poor old Rusty Wilson. As a kid, his divorcing parents decided his fate with a roll of the dice — below six, he'd live with his mum; above seven, he'd live with his dad. Now, as an adult, those same parents don't want to see him, he's lost his job and his wife's having an affair with an Uber driver.

It's fair to say Rusty's hit rock bottom. But that's where Australian author Steve Toltz (Booker-shortlisted for his 2008 debut A Fraction of the Whole) likes his characters to be.

Listen to the podcast Your favourite fiction authors share the stories behind their latest books on ABC Radio National's The Book Show.

Plot lovers, rejoice: this is a book where lots of stuff happens. And it's wild. Rusty's warring parents are unexpectedly reunited when they're kicked out of their respective nursing homes to live in Rusty's apartment; Rusty gets an ill-advised job as a school guidance counsellor (he tells the kids that AI has stolen their futures and sets them obscure philosophical homework); and he's reunited with a friend who is haunted by PTSD from her traumatic nightmares. It's weird and funny and deep — in other words, trademark Toltz.

A Rising of the Lights is set in a near-future Australia where robot nurses care for the elderly and a dour chatbot doles out relationship counselling. This has great comic potential, but Toltz also has some serious ideas to explore here: what will our purpose be, as technological advances make us wilfully redundant? And, in a world where an algorithm can tend to our broken hearts, is human connection more important than ever? Our narrator needs to confront his vulnerability and loneliness, and build relationships — even if it's with those rotten parents of his.

– Claire Nichols

Good Boy by Michelle Wright

Allen & Unwin

Wright became interested in criminal justice after appearing in a theatre production staged by inmates at Pentridge Prison as a university student. (Supplied: Allen & Unwin)

It's 1997, and with just a couple of months left on his sentence, Cookie is apprehensive about his looming freedom. He has become accustomed to keeping his head down, existing without connection or any sense of a future, living "on a three-day timeline: yesterday, today, tomorrow".

At a warden's suggestion, Cookie joins a program where inmates train abandoned dogs. The dogs that pass a behavioural test have the chance to be adopted, while those that fail are put down.

In quietly moving scenes, Cookie starts to warm to his allocated animal, Nigel, whom he soon renames Good Boy, partly to circumvent a rule that trainers can only praise their dogs once they complete a task. A keen student of psychology, Cookie sees something of himself in the anxious Good Boy. He believes the dog could pass the test with more time and support, yet the system is brutally inflexible.

Summer's best books Wondering what to read next? Buzzy debuts and lyrical literary fiction are among our critics' latest recommendations.

Unwilling to give up on Good Boy, Cookie makes a run from the low-security facility as the other prisoners watch Princess Diana's funeral, vowing to turn himself in as soon as he finds a safe home for the dog.

As the unlikely pair survive on their wits, the narrative stretches back to Cookie's bleak childhood. His mother left when he was an infant, leaving him to be raised by his father, a callous conman. Bullied at school, he gravitated towards Mrs Mitten, an empathetic school nurse and remedial class teacher who saw sensitivity and potential in Cookie where others saw unruliness.

Rendered in plainspoken prose that only heightens its heartbreaking power, Good Boy is a deeply moving work. Simultaneously a gripping tale of two world-weary outsiders learning to trust each other and a searing critique of how institutions fail those on the margins of society, it will stay with you long after its final page.

– Daniel Herborn

Transcription by Ben Lerner

Granta

"[Lerner] regards the digital moment as one in which our attention ... has been stolen and monetised," critic Geordie WIlliamson told ABC Radio National's The Bookshelf. (Supplied: Allen & Unwin)

First, props to Granta for a frankly fabulous cover. Look at that glossy black surface! Reflecting the face of you, the reader, back to yourself.

Swipe left on this particular touchscreen, though, and what greets you is not a dull parade of online advertising posing as information or entertainment, but a sly, funny, enigmatically provocative novel.

Ben Lerner's fourth, Transcription, begins with an unnamed narrator, a writer, travelling to meet his intellectual mentor, Thomas, on the occasion of Thomas's 90th birthday. Hoping to record the famous academic on his phone and then transcribe the results for the magazine interview he's been commissioned to carry out, he promptly drops his phone into the sink soon after checking in at his hotel.

Poetry collection wins $100k prize Eveyln Araluen has taken out the top award at the Victorian Premier's Literary Awards for The Rot.

Resolving to proceed with the interview anyway, he tells Thomas theirs will be a preliminary conversation before the recording proper. Freed from habitual recourse to his phone, he discovers himself experiencing a heightened sense of time and place; one that allows him to vividly recall his earlier life as an undergrad, the twist of fate that led to him meeting his wife — and her romantic (of sorts) predecessor — and to connect more deeply to his present, where he has a 10-year-old daughter, a girl who is refusing school — and who longs, like many of her classmates, for a smartphone of her own.

Like being added to a long-standing group chat, Lerner introduces many of the novel's narrative and thematic forces in the opening pages, albeit in ways that allow them to blossom more fully later on. An author known as much for his verse as his prose, it's an impressively compact novel that displays Lerner's poetic sensibilities.

Throughout Transcription, the question of what lasts — and what parts of our lives we might wish to make last — are juxtaposed with the risk of outsourcing our emotions, habits, attitudes, our entire lives and memories, to technology. (One running joke sees the narrator continually summon his phone for walking directions even when he already knows the route.)

Densely packed, Transcription rewards re-reading. Lerner suggests art is one of the purest forms of time travel, because it encourages the capacity to dream: an engine of creation no device can replace.

— Declan Fry

London Falling by Patrick Radden Keefe

Picador

In his latest book, Keefe — who won the Baillie Gifford Prize for Non-Fiction for his 2021 book Empire of Pain — investigates the death of a London teenager. (Supplied: Pan Macmillan Australia)

In the early hours of November 29, 2019, 19-year-old Zac Brettler fell to his death from the balcony of a luxury apartment overlooking the Thames in London.

Four years later, Patrick Radden Keefe — a staff writer at The New Yorker and author of several non-fiction titles, including Empire of Pain — learned about the teenager's mysterious death while in London on the set of the television adaptation of his 2018 bestseller, Say Nothing.

A friend of the Brettler family explained to Keefe how, unbeknownst to his middle-class Jewish parents, Zac had been living a double life, masquerading as the son of a Russian oligarch. Zac's concocted fortune, it emerges, earned him entrée into a dubious world of money and ostentation with links to the London underworld.

On losing a best friend to suicide Debra Adelaide became friends with Gabrielle Carey when they were 12. After Carey died by suicide five decades later, Adelaide tried to address her unanswered questions in a novel.

Zac's parents made the canny decision early on to make voice notes of their thoughts and recordings of any discussions relating to their son's death, including police interviews. Keefe draws from this huge and comprehensive archive, presenting much of the narrative in a close third-person point-of-view that gives the reader the sense of being in the room. The result is immersive and novelistic as we follow the same path of discovery as the grief-stricken Brettlers.

Keefe first wrote about Zac's death in a feature article published in The New Yorker in 2024. The author makes use of the book's expanded narrative to delve into London's recent history: the waves of immigration that have shaped the city and its transformation from a busy 19th-century trading port at the heart of a colonial empire to a global finance hub awash with dirty money.

— Nicola Heath

No Such Thing as Monday by Siân Hughes

Penguin

Kate Evans, speaking on ABC Radio National's The Bookshelf, described No Such Thing as Monday as "one of the best things that I've read this year". (Supplied" Penguin Books Australia)

British writer and poet Siân Hughes's first novel, Pearl — longlisted for the 2023 Booker Prize — was a story of lost mothers, mourning rituals, fathers getting by and houses, all connected through a medieval poem. It took Hughes more than a decade to write, rewrite and pare back that debut, and the result was painfully beautiful.

Her new novel seems, at first, to have an entirely different style. Tougher; brutal even, leavened with sharp humour. It's Steffie's story, told in first person, in working-class Birmingham. As the story opens, she is bringing her father his dinner, rushing out from her job in a dry cleaners — but he's dead in a chair, tethered to a vicious dog, and tethered to a long family history of violence and cock fighting and sneering control.

Listen to ABC RN's The Bookshelf The latest and best fiction reviewed by a team of dedicated bibliophiles.

As the narrative shifts between her new life, finally free of her obligations to her ungrateful father, and the past, we're given access to the childhood that brought her there: Thatcher's Britain and a series of 'unskilled' jobs that are, of course, highly skilled and precise, but wear her down.

There's more to it though, a strange shimmering absence in the story and Steffie's memories. Didn't she have a sister? Where did she go? And why was she absent from family meals, from any kindness? Why was she hidden behind a wall in the dark?

Meanwhile, Steffie "borrows" a set of clothes from the dry cleaners to wear to her father's funeral. Unfortunately, the outfit belongs to one of the funeral attendants, who glares at her throughout. Washing, ironing, memorising the chemicals and solvents that will get the marks out, Steffie, a wonderfully defiant character, wonders if she'll ever be clean of the stains of her own past — and in an author's note that lands like a kick to the stomach, we discover there's another 14th-century poem behind this novel, too, known as Purity or Cleanness. Prepare to be washed away.

– Kate Evans

The News From Dublin by Colm Tóibín

Picador Australia

Tóibín, a former Irish Laureate for Fiction, won the 2006 International Dublin Literary Award for his novel The Master. (Supplied: Pan Macmillan Australia)

One word kept coming to mind as I read the new collection of stories from Irish author Colm Tóibín: yearning.

But The News From Dublin does not concern itself with lovesick teens or happily-ever-after romances. Many readers will be familiar with Tóibín's popular novel Brooklyn — the tale of Irish immigration to New York, which was turned into a blockbuster film starring Saoirse Ronan — but don't be fooled into thinking the author serves up frivolous fare.

Combining the dark and moody traditions of Irish storytelling with the frank self-exposure characteristic of queer literature, Tóibín is the doyen of longing, and it echoes through every tale.

Colm Tóibín on his latest novel, Long Island The beloved Irish author has written a sequel to Brooklyn, but some readers aren't happy

In this collection, he focuses his emotional heft on lonely people all over the world who have been estranged from a person, place or time by the regular pitfalls and disappointments of adulthood.

You know these stories are going to hit you hard in the chest when the opener is about a woman learning her son has been killed at war and then journeying to the city to tell his widow. But this is not just maudlin for the sake of it.

Whether it's a man seeking the bliss of anonymity after being released from prison, an elderly woman finally taking a stand against her domineering family, or a father grappling with the injustice of immigration law, there's a real humanity to these characters, who are trying their best to deal with the very real griefs of living.

Many short story collections are best enjoyed by dipping in and out, but The News from Dublin is propulsive and raw, making it impossible to put down. And while the characters in each story are completely distinct from each other, that emotional through-line stitches the collection into something bigger, richer and all the more heartbreaking.

— Katherine Smyrk

Fruit Fly by Josh Silver

Oneworld

Silver grapples with questions of exploitation in Fruit Fly: "If I write about someone else's pain, am I appropriating it, or am I using it in a positive way to shine a light?" he told Dazed.

As Fruit Fly opens, the protagonist, Mallory, compares herself to an exploding piece of digital fruit in Candy Crush: "Here one moment, only to be pulverised into a spray of sweet nothing the very next. Obliterated. Forgotten." She's in crisis, and it sets the tone of what is a dark satire that delights in pushing its characters, and the reader, to the edge.

Mallory is a once-successful, 30-something writer, marooned by writer's block and married to handsome, controlling Ronan. They keep up appearances, living an enviable, seemingly perfect life in London's Crouch End. Leo is a young gay drug addict, living rough and selling his body for his next hit, with a talent for words himself. Worlds apart, the two are drawn into an unlikely symbiotic relationship. Mallory — inspired by the success of a fellow author's novel about a bisexual boy and a Reddit thread she reads, advising that "gay sells" and, to write a bestseller, to "go dark, make people cry" — sets up a Grindr account using her husband's photos and stumbles into Leo's orbit. For Mallory, it's a fruitful connection: "His story continues to surprise, and in stories, surprises are good."

The 'gay bogan love story' for all Holden Sheppard was feeling frustrated by writing restrictions being thrown at him so, with his latest novel, he's taken a completely different turn.

Mallory hijacks Leo's narrative, and Slay, her comeback novel, is born. She offers him therapy sessions; he accepts, planning to capitalise on her wealth. They're using each other, and Silver ensures neither escapes moral scrutiny when the inevitable fallout ensues.

Silver, a mental health nurse and YA author, covers serious ground in his debut adult novel: trauma exploitation, who has the right to tell whose story, domestic abuse, chemsex and addiction. It's a lot, and for the most part, it's convincing. Silver's alternating chapter structure, shifting between Mallory and Leo — including an effective one-off, mid-scene perspective swap — keeps it propulsive despite the darkness, providing glimpses of their inner feelings. Mallory is often reductive and sees life as a movie (she'd be played by Saoirse Ronan, Leo by Timothée Chalamet), while Leo performs vulnerability and pain, at one point labouring on his real trauma at an AA meeting before helping himself to the collection basket.

Partly inspired by RF Kuang's Yellowface and its skewering of literary morality, Fruit Fly is a bold and occasionally muddy exploration of who gets to hold the pen, figuratively and literally.

— Ying-Di Yin

Having Spent Life Seeking by Kae Tempest

Jonathan Cape

Tempest, a past winner of the Ted Hughes Award for his poetry, published his debut novel, The Bricks That Built the Houses, in 2016. (Supplied: Penguin Books Australia)

Kae Tempest is best known for his powerful poetry and spoken word performances — including a remarkable set at Glastonbury last year — and his fiction brings that same pain, joy and emotion to the page.

His second novel introduces us to Rothko (the nickname comes from the childhood red blush of their cheeks) who's relishing freedom after 15 years behind bars. Rothko, who is non-binary, is now in their 30s, and has returned to the British seaside town of Edgecliff where they grew up. They're working as a handyman, with a loyal dog for company, and avoiding the pub, where they know one drink could plunge them back into addiction.

Kae Tempest on shame and pride The British rapper, author and award-winning poet on why it took them years to accept their gender identity.

And that's not all they're trying to avoid. The spectre of Rothko's free-spirited, damaged mother Meg hangs over the town — Rothko does, and doesn't, want to see her. And Rothko also hasn't summoned the courage to contact Dionne, their one-time love, the bright spark that dulled the pain of their teenage years. A scene set in the past, where Dionne takes a young Rothko shopping for boxer shorts — so they no longer have to wear the ultra-feminine knickers their family buys them — is one of the most moving moments of the book.

There's a lot of darkness in Having Spent Life Seeking: poverty, addiction, discrimination, cruelty and neglect. But fans of Tempest will know to expect catharsis too. There is an inherent beauty in this story — for all their damage, Rothko is pure goodness. You'll care deeply for them, and the broken, beautiful people in their orbit.

– Claire Nichols

Sororicidal by Edwina Preston

Picador Australia

Preston is the author of a biography of the artist Howard Arkley and the 2022 novel Bad Art Mother. (Supplied: Pan Macmillan Australia)

Mary and Margot live in well-to-do circumstances in Adelaide in the early years of the 20th century. Each speaks in a sly and knowing voice, seeming to narrate their stories from a vantage point in the future that invites the reader in. ("Dicker was very gay, in the old-fashioned sense of the word").

Told in chapters alternating between each sister, the novel slowly reveals a peculiar world through the introduction of small and vibrant details. Together, they suggest a sense of something off-kilter in the girls' world, a black comedy of gothic violence bubbling beneath the surface.

The sadistic older sister Mary wields her authority and power over her younger, more impressionable sister, as the girls place hexes upon their enemies and studiously update a "Hate Book". Cruelty binds them, at least from Margot's perspective: "Being trusting was a weakness. Being poor was another. Being not us was definitely a weakness."

Sororicidal depicts not only the girls' external world but also their shared interior landscape. As children, their days are languorous, the sisters caught in a fantasy of curses and cruelties. It's a world Margot is reluctant to leave behind, not only because her body's physical transition to adulthood troubles her, but because she doesn't want to lose the childhood sense of gleeful anarchy she shares with her sister.

But grow up they do: Mary goes on to pursue a successful artistic career and becomes a more distant presence in her sister's life. As the narrative alternates between each sister's point of view, questions arise as to how shared their sense of the world ever really was.

The unlikely love-child of Jane Campion, Angela Carter and Barbara Hanrahan, Sororicidal is intelligent and stylish, full of dry wit and possessing an impressive sense of ambition and scope. As we follow each sister from youth to old age, Margot, in particular, sees some of her Sapphic opportunities vanish while the chance to pursue new possibilities diminishes with age. Yet, in spite of their complicated feelings of love and hate for each other, each woman's capacity to care for the other unexpectedly expands, a sororal bond borne of shared history.

— Declan Fry

Tune in to ABC Radio National at 10am Mondays for The Book Show and 10am Saturdays for The Bookshelf.

World.title: Is it ever OK to use someone else's toothbrush?
World.content:
Much to my partner's horror, on the odd occasion I have accidentally used his toothbrush.

And if I was ever stranded without my own — say I forgot to pack it for a weekend away — I'd totally be up for using his over forgoing brushing at all.

A small straw poll around the office shows many of us have done so in such circumstances.

Samantha Byrne, associate professor in oral biology at the University of Melbourne, says about half of us have shared a toothbrush — usually between spouses, or parents and children.

But it is OK to share a toothbrush in desperate times? Or are we better getting by with a bit of toothpaste on our finger?

What's living in our mouths and on our toothbrushes?

You can transfer viruses and bacteria through sharing a toothbrush. (Pexels)

There are more than 700 different bacterial species that can call the mouth home, but we are more likely to have about 200 bacterial species living in our mouths, along with some fungi and viruses, says Dr Byrne.

"Most of these are not harmful and in fact are probably beneficial in some way," she says.

The bacteria commonly found in the mouth that can be harmful, however, include Streptococcus mutans (often associated with tooth decay) and Porphyromonas gingivalis and Treponema denticola (associated with gum disease).

Dr Byrne says those diseases are largely preventable with good oral hygiene and diet.

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

The three species of bacteria mentioned above have also been found to live on toothbrushes.

Allowing your toothbrush to dry out between uses will ensure most bacteria transferred from your mouth die, Dr Byrne says.

"The microorganisms that are from your mouth, they are not really evolved to live on a toothbrush."

The more problematic bacteria usually come from the nasal passages, skin, hands and the bathroom itself (such as the ones that make it into the air from a flushing toilet), explains Dr Byrne.

They include Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli.

Is sharing a toothbrush riskier than kissing?

Probably not, according to Dr Byrne.

"The reality is if you are kissing somebody, sharing their toothbrush is probably not a huge leap to make," she says.

" If you live with someone, you are probably swapping those microorganisms anyway. "

Research suggests that 38 per cent of the oral microbiome is shared in couples living together – compared to only 3 per cent in couples who don’t live together.

Things get trickier if you have a blood-borne disease, explains Arosha Weerakoon.

Should you brush before or after brekkie? It's possible you've received conflicting advice from dentists over the years about whether to brush your teeth before or after your morning meal. We explain why.

She owns a dental practice and works as a senior lecturer at the University of Queensland.

"I actively discourage sharing a toothbrush," Dr Weerakoon says.

"Other than the fact we get a bit grossed out … blood-borne viruses like hepatitis B and hepatitis C can live on surfaces for a long time without a host."

She says we can transmit these when sharing a toothbrush, because brushing your teeth "usually causes at least some trauma to the gum".

You can also transmit viruses such as COVID, she says for example.

People who are immunocompromised need to be careful about sharing toothbrushes, warns Dr Byrne.

"[For example] someone who is undergoing chemo or an organ transplant, they need to be really careful with any microorganism they are exposed to."

Is sharing better than not brushing at all?

Dr Weerakoon says she would avoid sharing a toothbrush and look for alternative solutions if your own brush is absent.

For example, using some toothpaste and the corner of a towel to scrub your teeth.

Or at the very least, some toothpaste on your finger.

"For an added protective effect, chew some sugar-free gum to increase saliva," Dr Weerakoon says.

If you have some white vinegar handy, Dr Bryne says you could use that to disinfect another person's brush before sharing.

"A couple of studies show just 10 minutes in a 50/50 mix of water and white vinegar is quite effective. Cheap and easy."

Dr Byrne says one night of not brushing won't be detrimental to your oral health.

World.title: Prince Harry urges Putin to 'stop this war' on visit to Ukraine
World.content:
Britain's Prince Harry has called on Russia's President Vladimir Putin to end the war on a surprise visit to Kyiv, as the European Union unblocks a multi-billion-dollar loan to Ukraine.

The prince also urged US President Donald Trump to show leadership to help resolve the conflict, a week after a massive Russian aerial attack on Ukraine.

By convention, the British royal family do not speak out on political matters, although King Charles and other senior royals have regularly voiced their support for Ukraine.

But during Harry's Thursday visit, he used far more explicit language than any of his relatives had previously.

"President Putin, no nation benefits from the continued loss of life we are witnessing," Harry said in a speech to a Kyiv security forum.

"There is still a moment — now — to stop this war, to prevent further suffering for Ukrainians and Russians alike, and to choose a different course.

"This is a moment for American leadership, a moment for America to show that it can honour its international treaty obligations," he said.

Prince Harry says, "Europe has stood up in profound ways" in the war in Ukraine. (Reuters: Ministry of Veterans Affairs of Ukraine/Handout)

In his speech, which drew huge applause, he praised the Ukrainian people's resolve and the innovative response of its military, including its advanced drone capabilities.

"I am not here as a politician, I am here as a soldier who understands service, as a humanitarian who has seen the human cost of conflict, ⁠and as a friend of Ukraine who believes the world must not grow used to this war or numb to its consequences," Harry said.

Throwing Ukraine a lifeline

The European Union formally approved a 90-billion-euro ($148 ,billion) loan to Ukraine and new sanctions against Russia, ahead of an informal summit of the bloc's leaders in Cyprus which Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will attend.

EU backs $148bn loan for Ukraine A bitter feud over an oil pipeline pitted Hungary against Ukraine and stalled the vitally needed funds for Kyiv.

The loan is set to cover two-thirds of Ukraine's needs for the next two years.

Economists had said Ukraine would start ​to run out of money by June if the EU loan was not disbursed by then, requiring deep cuts to public services.

"We are on our way to Cyprus with good news," European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen said.

"While Russia doubles down on its aggression, we are doubling down on our support to the brave Ukrainian nation, enabling Ukraine to defend itself and putting pressure on Russia’s war economy."

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. (Reuters: Yves Herman)

EU ambassadors had already approved the loan and the sanctions package on Wednesday after Hungary lifted its veto, paving the way for the formal approval.

"This package will strengthen our army, make Ukraine more resilient, and enable us to fulfil our social obligations to Ukrainians, as set out in law," Mr Zelenskyy said on X.

"During meetings in Cyprus, we will also discuss with partners further sanctions pressure on Russia over this war. The 20th package has been unblocked, and it must be followed by other sanctions steps."

Russian diplomats denounced the sanctions, saying the new measures lacked UN legitimacy and infringed on the rights of third countries.

"We would like to remind you that only sanctions imposed by the decision of the UN Security Council are legitimate," state news agency TASS quoted the statement as saying.

"All others are unilateral coercive measures, and essentially, arbitrariness and aggression that contradict international law and the UN Charter."

Only half of the 90 billion euros will be disbursed to Ukraine this year, with the remainder coming in ​2027.

The bulk of the loan is earmarked for military spending, with about 17 billion euros each year destined for general budget needs such as health and education.

The loan's approval, delayed for several months by a veto by EU member Hungary, throws Kyiv a lifeline, averting deep cuts to public services, but the country may need more money to meet its military needs this year, economists and officials said.

ABC/Reuters

World.title: School crossing supervisor axing leaves parents fearing child safety
World.content:
Mother-of-three Karina Carless dreads the day a child is killed while crossing the road outside her local primary school.

She is one of several parents of students at Dunolly Primary School, in central Victoria, calling for the school's crossing supervisor role to be reinstated.

"I'm a CFA [Country Fire Authority] member, and I'm waiting for my pager to go off," Ms Carless said.

It is another service to be cut by the cash-strapped Central Goldfields Shire Council that is hoping to save $3.2 million in the next financial year by closing its tips in outlying towns and cutting labour costs.

The Department of Transport provides funding to councils to employ school crossing supervisors.

It uses an equation that requires a minimum of 20 students to use a school crossing and at least 100 vehicles to drive by in an hour.

The department and the council said just four students used the Dunolly crossing each day.

Parents say taking away the Dunolly supervised crossing exposes children to danger. (ABC News: Tyrone Dalton)

But parents say that figure is no longer correct after a growth in enrolments, and that child safety should be the most important consideration.

A council can request supervision on account of safety, such as excessive speed, road geometry, limited sight distance and the number of heavy vehicles.

The school's acting principal, Natalie Todeschini, said enrolment numbers at the school had grown to 87, up from 79 last year.

"I understand the concerns of the families and support them moving forward when considering building road safety infrastructure," she said.

The department said it did not receive a funding request from Central Goldfields Shire for the Dunolly site as part of its annual funding cycle.

Parents want the school crossing supervision role reinstated. (ABC News: Tyrone Dalton)

Parents say supervision needed

Dunolly is a small, former gold rush town in Central Victoria that is home to 899 people.

These days, it is cropping and transport that keep many of the town's residents employed.

Parents say that during harvest, the number of trucks that travel past the school can reach about 230.

Add in a crest just before the school zone, and they say it is a fatal accident waiting to happen.

"Ideally, nobody wants to be scraping a kid off the road," parent Megan Redpath said.

Ms Redpath said not having a crossing supervisor placed the onus on children to know and practice road safety.

"It's also not within their frame of responsibility," she said.

"At the moment, we barely even have flags out. Like, how do the people coming through know it's an operational crossing?"

Dunolly is a former gold rush mining town and is now home to 899 people. (Supplied: Rosemary Hiatt)

And Dunolly is not the only school facing cuts to school crossing supervision.

Last month, Campaspe Shire Council in northern Victoria cut the supervisor role from St Joseph's College Echuca because the Department of Transport said it would not continue to fund it, as not enough students used the crossing.

In a statement, Central Goldfields Shire Council said it would continue to communicate directly with the Dunolly Primary School regarding discussions with the Department of Transport and Planning.

It also urged motorists to slow down in school zones.

World.content:
Updated WorldEuropePrince Harry Prince Harry delivers messages for Trump, Putin on surprise Ukraine visit David Crowe Updated April 24, 2026 — 9:33am ,first published 5:35am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

London: Ukraine has gained a $147 billion funding boost to turn back Russian forces after a deadlock over European financial support, as Prince Harry conducts a surprise visit to Kyiv and calls for American leadership to end the war. The new funding comes as Ukrainian leaders harden their message about potential ceasefire terms, with presidential adviser Kyrylo Budanov declaring the country would not give up a “single millimetre” of its territory. Loading Russian military chief Valery Gerasimov claimed this week that Russia had taken 1700 square kilometres during the fighting so far this year, but expert observers dismissed the estimate and said Ukraine was inflicting significant damage on its enemy. Harry arrived in the Ukrainian capital with no public notice to address the Kyiv Security Forum, where he said he was speaking as a former soldier rather than a political figure.



In a message to US President Donald Trump and other American leaders, Harry said the US had been part of the assurance offered to Ukraine about its security when it gave up its nuclear weapons after the Cold War, leaving it exposed to Russian aggression today. “This is a moment for American leadership. A moment for America to show that it can honour its international treaty obligations,” he said. “Not out of charity, but out of its enduring role in global security and strategic stability.” Prince Harry at the Kyiv Security Forum on Thursday, after arriving in Ukraine earlier in the day. AP Trump dismissed the call and made a passing remark about the prince’s wife, Meghan Markle, the Duchess of Sussex. “Prince Harry? How’s his wife? Please give her my regards,” he said. “Prince Harry is not speaking for the UK, that’s for sure,” Trump said. “I think I’m speaking for the UK more than Prince Harry.”



The latest polling from YouGov found that 65 per cent of British voters disliked Trump, while only 16 per cent liked him and the others were neutral. Harry has also divided opinion, with a separate YouGov survey finding that 60 per cent had a negative view of him, while 30 per cent were positive. The prince has visited Ukraine several times, including visits to medical facilities such as the Superhumans centre in Lviv where soldiers are fitted with prosthetic limbs, given his work with the Invictus Games for soldiers with disabilities. In a message to Russian President Vladimir Putin, the prince said there was “still a moment” to stop the war now and choose a different course. Russia claims to be succeeding in the war and has gained temporary relief from US sanctions on its oil exports under a controversial decision by the Trump administration last week.



“Since the ​beginning of this year, a total of 80 settlements and more than 1700 square kilometres of territory have ​come under our control,” said Valery Gerasimov, chief of the general staff of the Russian forces, in comments reported by Reuters on Tuesday. Related Article Good Weekend The terrible need that propelled Ukraine to the top of this market The Institute for the Study of War, an independent non-profit group, dismissed Gerasimov’s claim as “greatly exaggerated” and said he was probably trying to obscure Russia’s lack of progress. A report by the institute early last month said Russia had occupied 19.4 per cent of Ukrainian territory, compared with 26.8 per cent shortly after the full-scale invasion in February 2022. “Subsequent Ukrainian counteroffensives left the Russians holding only about 17.9 per cent of Ukraine in November that year,” the institute said of the situation in 2022.



“Since then, Russia has seized only 1.5 per cent more Ukrainian land while suffering over 1 million casualties in total. Related Article Russia-Ukraine war Welcome to ‘Donnyland’: Ukraine proposes renaming territory in Trump’s honour “Russia has needed 3½ years to seize 9318 square kilometres, an area smaller than Lebanon or Los Angeles County.” The European Union ended months of dispute over funding for Ukraine by reaching a formal agreement in Cyprus on Thursday (late on Wednesday, AEST) to lend the country €90 billion (about $147 billion). The funding package was decided last year but blocked by Hungarian leader Viktor Orban under rules that required a consensus among leaders.



The election of a new Hungarian prime minister, Peter Magyar, cleared the way for the funds to be released, helped by a Ukrainian decision to resume oil flows from Russia to Hungary through a pipeline across its territory. Related Article Trump diplomacy ‘Throwing Russia lifeline after lifeline’: Latest US backflip delivers another blow to Ukraine “We have secured Ukraine’s financial resilience for two years,” said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky after the formal decision. EU leaders hailed the funding deal as a sign of unity against Russia, with French President Emmanuel Macron talking of a “more sovereign Europe” and Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal warning that peace would not come from compromise with the aggressor. “We will provide Ukraine what it needs to hold its ground, until Putin understands his war leads nowhere,” said EU foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas.



Trump sought to negotiate a peace deal with Putin, but the talks have dragged on without any substantial progress on Russia’s demand for large amounts of Ukrainian territory. Budanov, one of Zelensky’s top aides as head of the office of the president, said the negotiation process was sensitive and could not be disclosed, but he indicated there was no compromise on territory. “There will be no acceptance in Ukraine of losing even a single millimetre of our territory,” he told the Kyiv Security Forum. Harry speaks during a discussion with Ukrainian war veterans. AP Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: US soldier charged with using classified intel to win $560,000 bet on Maduro raid
World.content:
Breaking WorldNorth AmericaOnline gambling US soldier charged with using classified intel to win $560,000 bet on Maduro raid Hallie Golden and Konstantin Toropin April 24, 2026 — 9:32am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

Washington: A US soldier involved in the military operation to capture Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro has been charged with using classified information about the mission to win more than $US400,000 ($560,000) in an online betting market, federal officials announced. Gannon Ken Van Dyke was part of the operation to capture Maduro in January and allegedly used his access to classified information to make money on the prediction market site Polymarket, the federal prosecutor’s office in New York said on Thursday. A fire at Fort Tiuna, Venezuela’s largest military complex, after US strikes in the capital, Caracas, in January. AFP Van Dyke was involved in the planning and execution of capturing Maduro for about a month beginning on December 8, 2025, according to the federal prosecutor’s office. He signed nondisclosure agreements promising to not divulge “any classified or sensitive information” related to the operations, the office said. Officials allege that Van Dyke created a Polymarket account towards the end of December and made about 13 bets that took the “Yes” position on such wagers as US forces being in Venezuela and Maduro being out by January 31, 2026.



The soldier has been charged with unlawful use of confidential government information for personal gain, theft of non-public government information, commodities fraud, wire fraud and making an unlawful monetary transaction. Related Article Venezuela crisis Stealth drones and massive blowtorches: How the US mission to capture Maduro unfolded The case appeared to mark the first time the Department of Justice had brought insider trading charges involving a prediction market. FBI director Kash Patel said the announcement made it clear that no one was above the law. “Any clearance holders thinking of cashing in their access and knowledge for personal gain will be held accountable,” he said in a statement.



US President Donald Trump said he would investigate federal employees placing bets on event-betting platforms, indicating his concerns with prediction markets amid worries that individuals are using confidential government information to profit. “I’ll look into it,” Trump told reporters when asked on Thursday about the case against Van Dyke. Trump said he long had issues with the concept of event-betting platforms. A photo posted by US President Donald Trump to Truth Social shows Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro aboard the USS Iwo Jima after he was captured by US forces. Donald Trump / Truth Social “Well, you know, the whole world, unfortunately, has become somewhat of a casino,” Trump said. “And you look at what’s going on all over the world, in Europe and every place they’re doing these betting things. I was never much in favour of it. I don’t like it conceptually.” Trump said he was not familiar with the details of case but that it reminded him of Pete Rose, who was banned from Major League Baseball over a gambling scandal.



“That’s like Pete Rose betting on his own team,” Trump said. “If he bet against his team, that would be no good, but he bet on his own team.” Related Article Web culture A bar full of young things staring at TV screens. But they’re not watching football Van Dyk was a senior enlisted soldier who was part of the special forces community and stationed at Fort Bragg in Fayetteville, North Carolina, according to the indictment, but it offers little other details about his military service. He joined the army in 2008 and, in 2023, was promoted to the rank of master sergeant, the second-highest enlisted rank in the army, according to the indictment. However, the document says Van Dyke was photographed following the raid on the deck of a ship “wearing US military fatigues and carrying a rifle, standing alongside three other individuals wearing US military fatigues”.



Information on Van Dyke’s defence attorney was not immediately available. He is expected to face a judge in North Carolina later on Thursday (US time), the Department of Justice said. The Pentagon referred questions on the case to the army and the Department of Justice. US Special Operations Command did not immediately respond to requests for comment. In a post on X, Polymarket said it had referred the matter to the department. “Insider trading has no place on Polymarket. Today’s arrest is proof the system works,” the post read. World.title: This Netflix outback thriller can’t quite escape its own clichés
World.content:
★★★ CultureTV & radioStreaming This Netflix outback thriller can’t quite escape its own clichés Kylie Northover April 24, 2026 — 9:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

Apex ★★★ Rock climbing and other adventure sport films have been enjoying a moment recently, which must be as much a boon for drone videographers as for adrenaline fans. Once the domain of niche documentaries, extreme sports stories have surged since Free Solo, which won the Oscar for best documentary in 2019. The new Netflix film Apex combines that high-stakes action with an Australian “outback” thriller, as Charlize Theron and Taron Egerton face off in a classic game of cat-and-mouse. Charlize Theron as rock climber Sasha in Apex. Kane Skennar/NETFLIX © 2026 Theron is Sasha, an experienced climber who we first encounter scaling Europe’s tallest rock face, the Troll Wall in Norway, with her equally experienced partner Tommy (Eric Bana). They’re so seasoned that they can stop for a snog halfway up the famous “big wall”. But their ascent doesn’t go to plan, and five months later Sasha is in Australia and looking for some solace in nature. (Considering he’s not even featured in the film’s trailer, I don’t think it’s a spoiler to reveal that Sasha is grieving).



Related Article ★★★★★

Review Five stars for the fifth and final season of Hacks (after all, it’s what Deborah would want) The dusty roads, the tiny roadhouse and lack of mobile-phone coverage suggest Sasha is in the outback proper, but Australians will recognise the Blue Mountains as the fictional Wandarra National Park, home to popular climbing spots and rapid-filled waterways. After dealing with some ocker hunting stereotypes at the roadhouse, a more kindly local tells Sasha about an out-of-the-way camping spot, which can only be found using a paper map … you may well have an inkling where this is headed. Sasha spends an awkward evening hiding in her van from the dodgy hunters from the roadhouse, who turn up at her idyllic camping spot, and then spends the following day white-water kayaking. But when she wakes up the following morning her gear – including her food and mobile phone – has gone missing. Taron Egerton as Ben, who turns hunter, with Charlize Theron as Sasha, his prey. Kane Skennar/NETFLIX



Taking back to the water, she runs into Ben (Egerton), the nice guy who told her about the spot. But after offering her breakfast, Ben quickly turns into something entirely different, revealing he has Sasha’s bag, which he’s restocked, and a challenge: she has until the end of an incongruous Chemical Brothers song to get as far away as possible, then he’s coming after her with his crossbow. Sasha takes off into the bush, barefoot, and the rest of the film is a classic hunter-and-prey chase through an Australian tourism brochure. Editor's pick Spoilers

Streaming The Pitt is done for another season. Did fans ruin it for themselves? Egerton is suitably creepy as the skilled bushman (and he doesn’t do a bad Aussie accent), making unnerving screeching and trilling noises as he pursues Sasha on land, over rapids and into caves. Theron is serviceable as the ultra-fit prey who gives as good as she gets. Directed by Baltasar Kormakur, who’s become something of a specialist in nature/survival films such as Everest and Adrift, Apex looks great (some obvious CGI aside), and has a frenetic pace when Ben and Sasha are on the move. But there are too many clichés and too few surprises. Both Sasha (steely resolve, tougher than she’s given credit for) and Ben (mummy issues, loner) feel flatter than the face of the Troll Wall. If you’re happy, though, with foothold-related tension and Solo Man-style kayak action, get your aqua socks on and strap in.
